title: Cassandra Deep Dive
description: Master Cassandra internals: gossip protocol, virtual nodes, Merkle tree repair, tunable consistency levels, and compaction strategies (STCS/LCS/TWCS).

segments.text: Cassandra is a masterless distributed database — no single point of failure. Every node is equal. Netflix runs over ten thousand Cassandra nodes storing petabytes of data. The key design choices: eventual consistency by default, tunable consistency per query, and linear horizontal scaling. Understanding its internals is essential for any Staff-level interview.

Gossip protocol: every second, each node picks a random peer and exchanges state — which nodes are alive, their load, their token ranges. After a few rounds, all nodes converge on the same cluster view. It's eventually consistent but extremely fault-tolerant — even during network partitions, the healthy partition maintains correct membership.

Virtual nodes solve the hot-spot problem. Instead of each physical node owning one token range, it owns two hundred fifty-six virtual tokens spread around the ring. This distributes data evenly and makes rebalancing fast — when a new node joins, it takes a few virtual tokens from each existing node rather than a large chunk from one neighbor.

Tunable consistency per query. ONE: acknowledge after one replica writes — fast, risk of stale reads. QUORUM: majority must acknowledge — balanced. ALL: every replica must acknowledge — slowest, strongest consistency. The formula: R plus W greater than N guarantees strong consistency. QUORUM read plus QUORUM write with replication factor three achieves this.

Your application uses consistency level ONE for reads and writes with replication factor three. This means a read might return stale data. Under what circumstances is this acceptable, and when would you need QUORUM?
segments.thought_prompt: When is eventual consistency (CL ONE) acceptable vs when must you use QUORUM?

segments.text: Merkle tree repair — called anti-entropy repair — detects and fixes data inconsistencies between replicas. Each node builds a hash tree over its data ranges. Nodes exchange tree hashes — differing subtrees identify inconsistent ranges. Only the inconsistent data is transferred. Run full repairs at least once within gc_grace_seconds — default ten days — to prevent zombie data resurrection.

Size-Tiered Compaction Strategy groups SSTables of similar size and merges them. Small tables merge into medium, medium into large. Good for write-heavy workloads — it minimizes write amplification. But temporary space usage can reach double the data size during compaction. This is Cassandra's default and works well for most use cases.

Leveled Compaction Strategy maintains fixed-size SSTables in levels. Level zero feeds into level one with ten times the capacity. Read performance is excellent — each key exists in at most one SSTable per level. Time-Window Compaction Strategy groups SSTables by time window — perfect for time-series data where old data is rarely updated. Choose TWCS for time-series, LCS for read-heavy, STCS for write-heavy.

Cassandra data modeling is query-driven — design tables around your access patterns, not around entities. Denormalize aggressively. A single query should hit a single partition. If you need data by user ID and by email, create two tables with different partition keys. This feels wrong coming from relational databases, but it's essential for Cassandra performance.

You're designing a Cassandra schema for a messaging application. Messages must be queryable by conversation ID in time order and by user ID for inbox view. How many tables do you need, and what are their partition keys?
segments.thought_prompt: Design Cassandra tables for chat messages queryable by conversation and by user inbox.

segments.text: Cassandra's architecture — masterless gossip, virtual nodes, tunable consistency, Merkle tree repair, and pluggable compaction — makes it ideal for write-heavy, globally distributed workloads. The trade-off: query flexibility is limited to your table design. Model your data around queries, choose the right compaction strategy for your workload, and run repairs regularly.
